title: Nonadiabatic dynamics under slow parametric modulation in nonlinear graphene resonators
authors: Chris F. D. Wattjes, Haemin Lim, Pierpaolo Belardinelli, John E. Sader, Peter G. Steeneken, Farbod Alijani
abstract: Resonantly driven nonlinear systems, from superconducting circuits to nanomechanical resonators, are often described in a rotating frame, where amplitude and phase evolve slowly within a fixed landscape of stable and unstable states. How such systems behave when this landscape moves on their intrinsic timescale remains to be understood. Here, we exploit the strong tension sensitivity of a graphene drum's resonance frequency to reshape the rotating-frame phase space of a bistable mechanical mode in real time, combining an MHz-frequency resonant drive with kHz-frequency tension modulation. When the modulation rate becomes comparable to the mechanical relaxation rate, adiabatic tracking of the fixed points breaks down. Instead, parametric instabilities emerge in the slow dynamics at frequencies set by libration around these points rather than by the mechanical resonance; stronger modulation drives period doubling and chaos. A slow-variable theory predicts where the instabilities occur, and Melnikov analysis captures the onset of chaos. These results show that the rotating frame itself can be parametrically driven, offering a general route to controlling nonadiabatic dynamics in systems ranging from Josephson bifurcation amplifiers to cold atoms.
summary: This work demonstrates how parametric modulation of a nonlinear graphene resonator can drive its phase space in real time, moving beyond simple external forcing. By analyzing the competition between modulation and relaxation timescales, the authors predict and observe transitions into parametric instability and chaos. This offers a general method for controlling nonadiabatic dynamics in various physical systems.
main_problem: The paper investigates nonadiabatic dynamics in nonlinear systems when the underlying phase-space structure itself evolves in time due to slow parametric modulation.
main_result: The system transitions from adiabatic tracking of fixed points to parametric instabilities and chaos when the modulation rate becomes comparable to the system's intrinsic relaxation rate.
method: The study combines experimental measurements on graphene resonators with theoretical tools like slow-variable theory, Melnikov analysis, and Lyapunov exponent calculations.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a nonlinear graphene resonator (drum) driven by a fast MHz resonant drive and a slow kHz parametric modulation of its tension. The dynamics are modeled by a Duffing-Mathieu type equation.
key_observables: Bistability, period-doubling, chaotic motion, Lyapunov exponents ($\lambda_{max}$), and the Poincaré section structure.
important_parameters: The ratio between the modulation rate ($\omega_S$) and the mechanical relaxation rate ($\Gamma$) is critical for determining the dynamic regime.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the strong tension sensitivity of the graphene resonance frequency, and approximations are made by transforming to a rotating frame and using averaging methods.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup, the transition from adiabatic following to instability, and the quantitative detection of chaos using Lyapunov exponents and bifurcation diagrams across multiple experimental setups.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical problem and the experimental setup (graphene resonator) to developing the mathematical model (Duffing-Mathieu equation in a rotating frame). It then analyzes the three dynamic regimes (adiabatic, delayed, chaotic) using advanced tools like Melnikov analysis and Lyapunov exponents, concluding with validation on multiple physical realizations.
why_interesting: The concept of parametrically driving the rotating frame itself provides a general, controllable mechanism for inducing nonadiabatic dynamics, which is highly relevant for controlling quantum systems where the Hamiltonian parameters are time-dependent.
